Let’s first consider the “Intercept”. This parameter is largely the ratio of used to available sample. If we increase our available sample, this estimate will get smaller. Its value has a lot to do with how we setup the data to approximate the true underlying model. It has no biological interpretation, so we can skip it.
Next, we have estimated the effect of “for500” as -0.68. This estimate is negative, indicating that as the value of “for500” increases from its mean (defined at 0) while the values of forest and shrub (the other variables in the model) are held at their mean that habitat selection decreases. In other words, habitat use relative to what is available to this individual (as we defined it!) decreases the greater the proportion of forest. That’s a lot of qualifiers to understand this estimate. These are important though. In terms of evidence of an effect, we can say that at a defined probability of Type I error of 0.05, we have a statistically clear effect and that that it is not likely zero. The evidence of this is the very small p-value of ?.
Next, we have estimated the effect of forest as 0.12. This estimate is positive, indicating that as the value of forest increases from its mean (defined at 0) while the values of dist.dev and shrub (the other variables in the model) are held at their mean that habitat selection increases relative to what is available to this individual. At our defined Type I error we do not have statistical clarity and there is a reasonable chance that it is zero. (p-value = 0.4665834).
Next, we have estimated the effect of shrub as 0.88. This estimate is positive, indicating that as the value of shrub increases from its mean (defined at 0) while the values of dist.dev and forest (the other variables in the model) are held at their mean that habitat selection increases relative to what is available to this individual. At our defined Type I error we do have statistical clarity of an effect that is not zero (p-value = 8.2627753^{-7}).
Relative Selection
How do we quantitatively evaluate two locations in terms of habitat selection using our model results? We can do so using Equation 8 of Fieberg et al. 2021.
Perhaps we want to compare a location that is very near development (dist.dev = -2) at high forest and shrub cover (forest = 2, shrub = 2) with that of a location far from development (dist.dev = 2) and also at high forest but low shrub cover (forest =2, shrub = -2).

1084.895 


If given equivalent availability between these two types of sites ( 1) near development at high forest and shrub cover, 2) far from development at high forest and shrub cover ), this individual would relatively select the first location by a factor of 2801.05.
Why are we exponentiating our linear combinations of terms (additions of covariates times estimated coefficients)? This is because in this setup, we have assumed the habitat selection process follows an exponential form (see section 10. The model being approximated) and equation 1 of Gerber and Northrup, 2020.
Relative Selection Strength
Avgar et al. 2017 refers to the relative selection strength (RSS) as the exponentiation of each coefficient.
For example,


  fp.dist 
0.5789681 


Given two locations that differ by 1 standard deviation of dist.dev, but are otherwise equal, this individual would be 1.1324727 as likely to choose the location with higher dist.dev (or, equivalently, 0.8830235 times more likely to choose the location with the lower dist.dev.





















Lets combine our covariates now to predict relative habitat selection over more scenarios. To do this, we need to remember we used generalized linear modeling functions to approximate our model. We need to take care when predicting. First, we need to remember to drop the intercept. Second, we need to remember our true link function for relative habitat selection is the log-link (inverse-link is the exponential function) and not the logit-link, which is the default when fitting logistic regression models.
fp.dist









We see that for this individual, given equal availability and forest and shrub at their mean values, avoid areas far from development (high values on x-axis) and select for areas close to development (low values on x-axis).
We can use this same process to extract values across spatial layers to predict relative habitat selection that is mapped.

Estimating the boundaries of seasonal and annual caribou ranges is an important step in effective wildlife conservation and management. The why and how of estimating ranges is discussed further in the Ranges appendix. In this section, we first illustrate the approach for estimating individual- and population level annual and seasonal ranges. We then use the output to answer a few questions of interest. For full access to the results, we invite the user to visit the Range Viewer dashboard.



In this section we describe the steps used to estimate individual home ranges using the KDE approach and compare it to another commonly used method, the minimum convex hull (MCP). We illustrate the approach for one individual caribou.














Tracks are the basic building blocks of movement analysis in the amt package. So, we first use the make_track function for convert our data.frame into tracks. Note that we have to specify the crs of the data which, in this case, is lat-long or “EPSG:4326”. We can then project our coordinates to the Yukon Albers projection using the transform_coords function.












Geometric estimators: MCP
Geometric estimators such as minimum convex polygons(MCP) only rely on the observed locations and can only estimate the occurrence distribution (i.e., where the animal was during the study period). MCPs can be constructed with multiple levels using the function hr_mcp() from the amt package.
Estimated home range area for each level:


# A tibble: 4 × 3
  level what       area
  <dbl> <chr>    [km^2]
1  1    estimate  3148.
2  0.95 estimate  3134.
3  0.75 estimate  2666.
4  0.5  estimate  1944.


MCPs can be viewed as isopleths.









Probabilistic estimators (KDE)
Probabilistic estimators (e.g., KDEs) are based on an underlying model for the utilization distribution (UD). They can estimate the occurrence distribution or the range distribution (where the animal could be found at any future time if its movement process remains the same) depending on the underlying model. Can be represented as a hull by outlining a cumulative probability of use. Fitting a KDE to telemetry data is the same problem as with MCPs, but in 2 dimensions. Choosing a bandwidth is important to the final result, and there are multiple possible methods for doing so. Here, we will focus on the reference bandwidth, whic is the default.


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  level what            area
  <dbl> <chr>          <dbl>
1  0.95 estimate 6768435375.
2  0.5  estimate 1521379550.


Unlike MCPs, KDEs include two additional raster objects:

‘ud’ – the rasterized utilization distribution
‘trast’ – the template raster used to rasterize the UD

Here we make a plot with the 50% and 95% isopleths drawn over the UD raster.









Autocorrelated KDE (AKDE)

























We can now compare the overlap in estimated ranges between the two methods:


Code
#hr_isopleths(mcp1)
ovr1 <- hr_overlap(mcp1, kde1)
ovr2 <- hr_overlap(kde1, mcp1)
tibble(
  Overlap = c("MCP estimate overlaps KDE estimate by:", "KDE estimate overlaps MCP estimate by:"),
  `Overall area (95%)` = c(round(ovr1$overlap[1]*100,1), round(ovr2$overlap[1]*100,1)),
  `Overall area (50%)` = c(round(ovr1$overlap[2]*100,1), round(ovr2$overlap[2]*100,1))) |>

title: Estimating ranges
text:
Walkthrough
In this section we describe the steps used to estimate individual home ranges using the KDE approach and compare it to another commonly used method, the minimum convex hull (MCP). We illustrate the approach for one individual caribou.


Code
library(sf)
library(amt)
library(tmap)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)



Step 1. Read locations


Code
gps <- read_csv('../../data/little_rancheria/caribou.csv')
gps1 <- gps |> filter(id=="SKRATALR0043" & year==2022)
gps1_sf <- gps1 |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("longitude", "latitude"), crs=4326, remove=FALSE) |>
  mutate(year=as.factor(year))
tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(gps1_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill="red")











Step 2. Make tracks
Tracks are the basic building blocks of movement analysis in the amt package. So, we first use the make_track function for convert our data.frame into tracks. Note that we have to specify the crs of the data which, in this case, is lat-long or “EPSG:4326”. We can then project our coordinates to the Yukon Albers projection using the transform_coords function.


Code
trk <- make_track(gps, longitude, latitude, timestamp, id=id, year=year, season=season, crs=4326)
trk1 <- make_track(gps1, longitude, latitude, timestamp, id=id, year=year, season=season, crs=4326)
trk1_sf <- trk1 |>
  group_by(id, year) |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("x_", "y_"), crs=4326) |>
  summarize(do_union=FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING") |>
  st_make_valid()
tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(trk1_sf) +
  tm_lines(lwd=2) +
  tm_shape(gps1_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill="red")











Step 3. Estimate ranges
Geometric estimators: MCP
Geometric estimators such as minimum convex polygons(MCP) only rely on the observed locations and can only estimate the occurrence distribution (i.e., where the animal was during the study period). MCPs can be constructed with multiple levels using the function hr_mcp() from the amt package.
Estimated home range area for each level:


Code
mcps <- hr_mcp(trk1, levels = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.95, 1))
hr_area(mcps, units = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(area = units::set_units(area, "km^2"))


# A tibble: 4 × 3
  level what       area
  <dbl> <chr>    [km^2]
1  1    estimate  3148.
2  0.95 estimate  3134.
3  0.75 estimate  2666.
4  0.5  estimate  1944.


MCPs can be viewed as isopleths.


Code
iso1 <- hr_isopleths(mcps) |>
  mutate(level = factor(level))
tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(gps1_sf) +
  tm_dots() +
  tm_shape(iso1) +
  tm_borders(col="level", col.scale=tm_scale(values=c("red","darkgreen","blue","black")), lwd=2, col.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_add_legend(title="MCP Level", labels=c("50%","75%","95%","100%"), col=c("red","darkgreen","blue","black"), 
    fill_alpha=0, position = tm_pos_in(pos.v = "bottom", pos.h="right"))

Probabilistic estimators (e.g., KDEs) are based on an underlying model for the utilization distribution (UD). They can estimate the occurrence distribution or the range distribution (where the animal could be found at any future time if its movement process remains the same) depending on the underlying model. Can be represented as a hull by outlining a cumulative probability of use. Fitting a KDE to telemetry data is the same problem as with MCPs, but in 2 dimensions. Choosing a bandwidth is important to the final result, and there are multiple possible methods for doing so. Here, we will focus on the reference bandwidth, whic is the default.


Code
kde1 <- hr_kde(trk1, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))
hr_area(kde1)


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  level what            area
  <dbl> <chr>          <dbl>
1  0.95 estimate 6768435375.
2  0.5  estimate 1521379550.


Unlike MCPs, KDEs include two additional raster objects:

‘ud’ – the rasterized utilization distribution
‘trast’ – the template raster used to rasterize the UD

Here we make a plot with the 50% and 95% isopleths drawn over the UD raster.


Code
kde1 <- hr_kde(trk1, levels = c(0.5, 0.95))
kde1i <- kde1 |>
  hr_isopleths()
tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(kde1i) +
  tm_borders(col="black", lwd=2, lty="dashed") +
  tm_polygons( 
    fill="level", fill.scale=tm_scale(values=c("yellow","darkgreen")),
    fill_alpha=0.5, fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_add_legend(
    title = "KDE", labels = c("Core (50%)", "Overall (95%)"), fill=c("yellow","darkgreen"), fill_alpha=0.75, position = tm_pos_in(pos.v = "bottom", pos.h="right"))









Autocorrelated KDE (AKDE)


Code
akde1 <- hr_akde(trk1, levels=c(0.5, 0.95)) # uses an iid ctmm
#akde1 <- hr_akde(trk1, model = fit_ctmm(trk1, "ou")) # uses an OU ctmm
akde1i <- akde1 |>
  hr_isopleths()
tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(akde1i) +
  tm_borders(col="black", lwd=2, lty="dashed") +
  tm_polygons( 
    fill="level", fill.scale=tm_scale(values=c("yellow","darkgreen")),
    fill_alpha=0.5, fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_add_legend(
    title = "KDE", labels = c("Core (50%)", "Overall (95%)"), fill=c("yellow","darkgreen"), fill_alpha=0.75, position = tm_pos_in(pos.v = "bottom", pos.h="right"))

Let’s first consider the “Intercept”. This parameter is largely the ratio of used to available sample. If we increase our available sample, this estimate will get smaller. Its value has a lot to do with how we setup the data to approximate the true underlying model. It has no biological interpretation, so we can skip it.
Next, we have estimated the effect of “for500” as -0.68. This estimate is negative, indicating that as the value of “for500” increases from its mean (defined at 0) while the values of forest and shrub (the other variables in the model) are held at their mean that habitat selection decreases. In other words, habitat use relative to what is available to this individual (as we defined it!) decreases the greater the proportion of forest. That’s a lot of qualifiers to understand this estimate. These are important though. In terms of evidence of an effect, we can say that at a defined probability of Type I error of 0.05, we have a statistically clear effect and that that it is not likely zero. The evidence of this is the very small p-value of ?.
Next, we have estimated the effect of forest as 0.12. This estimate is positive, indicating that as the value of forest increases from its mean (defined at 0) while the values of dist.dev and shrub (the other variables in the model) are held at their mean that habitat selection increases relative to what is available to this individual. Next, we have estimated the effect of shrub as 0.88. How do we quantitatively evaluate two locations in terms of habitat selection using our model results? We can do so using Equation 8 of Fieberg et al. 2021.
Perhaps we want to compare a location that is very near development (dist.dev = -2) at high forest and shrub cover (forest = 2, shrub = 2) with that of a location far from development (dist.dev = 2) and also at high forest but low shrub cover (forest =2, shrub = -2).

title: Identifying corridors
text:
Walkthrough
In this section we describe the steps used to estimate individual home ranges using the KDE approach and compare it to another commonly used method, the minimum convex hull (MCP). We illustrate the approach for one individual caribou.


Code
library(sf)
library(amt)
library(tmap)
library(terra)
library(tidyverse)



Step 1. Identify migration periods
This step is described in “Seasonal migrations” in the “Defining segments” section.


Step 2. Map individual paths
Simply connecting the dots of a migration sequence with a straight line gives a rough idea of the route, but it’s an oversimplification. It doesn’t reveal the true width of the path or, more importantly, the specific areas where an animal stopped-over to rest and feed. To build a more realistic map, we used a statistical method called the Brownian Bridge Movement Model (BBMM). This model is incorporates a key parameter called the Brownian motion variance (BMV), which is a statistical estimate of an individual’s mobility, making the resulting map more realistic. The output of this model is a utilization distribution (UD), which is essentially a “heat map” or “probability surface.” Instead of just showing a line, the UD shows the likelihood of an individual having been in any given location along its route. The “hotter” the color, the more time the individual likely spent there.
Using a BBMM to create a utilization distribution has two major benefits:

Estimates path width: The model calculates the probable width of the movement path around the straight lines connecting the points. This transforms a simple line into a more realistic two-dimensional corridor, showing the full area the individual may have used.
Identifies stopover sites: The “hottest” parts of the heat map are incredibly valuable. They reveal stopover sites - critical areas where animals spend extended time foraging and resting during their long journey. These sites are as important to the success of a migration as the path itself.



Code
gps <- read_csv("../../data/little_rancheria/caribou.csv")
aoi <- st_read("../../data/little_rancheria/corridors.gpkg", "aoi", quiet=TRUE)

# Spring
gps1s <- gps |> filter(id=="SKRATALR0018" & year==2021 & migration=="Spring migration")
gps1s_sf <- gps1s |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("longitude", "latitude"), crs=4326, remove=FALSE)
xs <- st_read("../../data/little_rancheria/corridors.gpkg", "bbmm95", quiet=TRUE) |>
  filter(id=="43141" & year==2021 & migration=="Spring migration")

# Fall
gps1f <- gps |> filter(id=="SKRATALR0018" & year==2021 & migration=="Fall migration")
gps1f_sf <- gps1f |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("longitude", "latitude"), crs=4326, remove=FALSE)
xf <- st_read("../../data/little_rancheria/corridors.gpkg", "bbmm95", quiet=TRUE) |>
  filter(id=="43141" & year==2021 & migration=="Fall migration")

ms <- tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(aoi) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(xs) +
  tm_polygons(fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_shape(gps1s_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill="red") +
  tm_title("Spring migration")
mf <- tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(aoi) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(xf) +
  tm_polygons(fill.legend = tm_legend_hide()) +
  tm_shape(gps1f_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill="red") +
  tm_title("Fall migration")
tmap_arrange(ms, mf)





Figure 1. Brownian bridge movement model (95% contour) for one caribou in 2021.






Step 3. Average individual paths
To protect a migration, we need to see the main corridor used by the entire population, not just the path of one individual. This can be achieved this by combining all the individual maps into a single, comprehensive view of the herd’s movement. This involves a three step process:

Average individual migrations: First, for each individual, we took all of its yearly migration UDs (the heat maps) and average them together. This creates a single map representing the typical migration path for that specific animal over time.
Define individual footprints: For each animal’s averaged map, we defined its “footprint” as the area that contains 99% of its probable locations. This captures the vast majority of where that individual traveled.
Stack the footprints: All of these individual footprints are then layered, or “stacked” on top of one another. The result is a map where every pixel on the grid has a value corresponding to how many different individuals passed through it.



Code
rs <- rast("../../data/little_rancheria/spring_migration.tif")
ms <- tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(aoi) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(rs) +
  tm_raster(col.legend = tm_legend(
    title = "Caribou use", position = tm_pos_in(pos.v = "bottom", pos.h="right"))) +
  tm_title("Spring migration")
rf <- rast("../../data/little_rancheria/fall_migration.tif")
mf <- tm_basemap("Esri.WorldTopoMap") +
  tm_shape(aoi) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(rf) +
  tm_raster(col.legend = tm_legend(
    title = "Caribou use", position = tm_pos_in(pos.v = "bottom", pos.h="right"))) +
  tm_title("Fall migration")
tmap_arrange(ms, mf)





Figure 2. Movement paths based on BBMM models for all caribou in all years.






Step 4. Classify corridors
Finally, we can classify the resultant stacked map to visualize how 1) intensely different parts of the corridor are used by the herd and 2) where the key stopovers areas are located. This allows us to distinguish between occasional and essential parts of the corridor.
Output 1: Corridor use intensity
The levels of corridor use are typically defined as follows:








Use Level
Definition
Importance




Low Use
Areas used by at least one individual.
Shows the maximum extent of the entire migration footprint.


Medium Use

title: Caribou Analysis and Modelling
text:
Caribou play an important role for LFN, serving as a keystone species in local ecosystems and having cultural significance for Indigenous communities. Ecologically, caribou contribute to the health of boreal forests by influencing vegetation patterns and providing food for predators. Culturally, caribou provide food, materials for clothing and tools, and are a central part of local traditions and knowledge. Consequently, the conservation of their seasonal ranges, including winter foraging grounds and summer calving and grazing areas, is important for the health and long-term persistence of the population. However, these habitats are increasingly threatened by human activities and disturbances, particularly large-scale resource development like mining, which leads to habitat fragmentation and landscape alteration.
The establishment of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) and other protected lands are important tools for ensuring the long-term survival of caribou populations, as they allow for the management of these threats. These areas enable collaborative stewardship, respect traditional ecological knowledge, and support sustainable use, thus contributing to the persistence of caribou and their habitats. By prioritizing both ecological integrity and cultural continuity, IPCAs can thus strengthen conservation and sustainable land management now and in the future. As part of this project, we will evaluate the contribution of the proposed IPCAs to seasonal movements, habitat selection, and landscape connectivity.

Although the Yukon Government also provides definitions fpr spring and fall migration periods, we decided, due to the large variation in movement patterns, to identify seasonal migration periods for each individual for each year. To do this we used Net Squared Displacement (NSD) analysis combined with visual inspection of the spatial distribution of GPS locations using the BEACONs Movement Mapper app to identify spring and fall migration start and end dates for each individual in each year. Migration periods were defined as follows:

Spring migration: Movement from winter range to summer range (generally northeast direction), beginning when individuals depart the winter range and ending upon arrival at summer range
Fall migration: Movement from summer range to winter range (generally southwest direction), beginning when individuals depart the summer range and ending upon arrival at winter range



We used the Movement Mapper app to identify start and end dates for spring and fall migration periods for each individual in each year.

For each individual/year:

Visualize movement tracks on map with seasonal color coding
Review NSD vs. day-of-year plots
Identify migration periods using these criteria:

Spring migration start: First sustained increase in NSD (e.g., >20% increase maintained for >7 days)
Spring migration end: NSD plateau or reversal indicating arrival at summer range
Fall migration start: First sustained decrease in NSD from summer range
Fall migration end: NSD plateau indicating establishment on winter range

Adjust date sliders to refine start/end dates based on visual assessment
If clear spring and fall migrations exist: Record start/end dates for both periods
If no evidence of migration assign NA to migration dates
Document ambiguous cases with comments in the notes field


Notes:
The first challenge in mapping a migration is figuring out when an animal is actually migrating versus when it is simply living in its seasonal home range. An individual caribou might wander for several kilometres in its summer territory, but that isn’t the same as its focused, directional journey between seasons. To solve this, we can use analytical tool called Net Squared Displacement (NSD). In simple terms, NSD measures the straight-line distance an animal is from a fixed starting point, which is typically set near the beginning of the biological year (e.g., January 1) within the animal’s winter range, and then squares that value. When plotted on a graph over a full year, the NSD curve for a migrating animal reveals a distinct, three-phase pattern:

In the starting range: When an individual is settled in its winter or summer range, it stays relatively close to the starting point. The NSD value fluctuates a little but remains low, creating a relatively flat line on the graph.
During migration: As the individual begins its journey to its summer or winter range, it moves steadily away from the starting point. This causes the NSD value to increase sharply and consistently, creating a steep upward slope on the graph.
In the target range: Once the individual arrives and settles in its summer or winter range, it is far from the starting point, so the NSD value is high. However, because it is no longer moving in a single direction, the value stabilizes and flattens out again at this new, higher level.

The “clear breakpoints” on the graph – where the line begins to rise and where it flattens out – allow us to identify the exact start and end dates of the spring and fall migrations. All the locations recorded between these dates are then grouped together, forming a single “migration sequence” for that animal in that year.

Guidelines for getting the basics right (Gerber et al. preprint)

Think thoroughly about the question(s) of interest and the appropriate geographic and temporal scales in the specific study system before data collection begins.


Which groups or classes are of interest in your system? Are you planning to break up the dataset by age/sex class/study area? How many individuals of each group must be sampled?


Define availability and determine whether you want to fit a HSF or SSF


Are you interested in identifying where individuals select home ranges (second order HSF) or locations within that home range (third order HSF) or along a movement path (SSF)?


Decide whether you are interested in inference or prediction and how that impacts model building


Inference is most straightforward when a single model is used with all relevant variables that capture the hypotheses of interest; it is important that the mechanisms motivating variables are given great thought. Prediction will often be improved by considering many models and does not necessarily require clear mechanisms behind including variables.


Understand and acknowledge the assumptions underlying your specific analysis


Assumption of an exponential selection function that forces inference to the relative intensity of selection or relative probability of selection.
Logistic regression and conditional logistic regression are used to approximate the underlying spatial or spatio-temporal point process model, respectively.


Conduct a sensitivity analysis for availability sample size.


Fit the model, examine the estimated selection coefficients, and then do the whole exercise again with a larger number of sampled available points. If the selection coefficients do not change, the original number of available points sampled was sufficient. If they do change, keep repeating the exercise until they do not.


Account for animal behavior and heterogeneity in your analysis


How quickly can the animal of interest move? Available locations from an animal location that are more than this distance within the considered time frame are not realistically available to the animal.
Is it reasonable to consider consecutive points on an individual’s track independent or are they temporally autocorrelated? It is important to account for this autocorrelation either by using a SSF, weighting techniques (Alston et al. 2022), or data thinning.
Ecological literature leads us to a priori consider individual variation, which is an important source of variation, and thus our main sampling unit is the individual. When individuals are tracked, pooling data across individuals and ignoring individual variation leads to poor statistical conclusions. Accounting for individual level differences can be accounted for using a full random effects (intercept and slopes) structure.
Consider all animal locations with regard to behavior and contextual environments (e.g., diel period, life stage, reproductive behaviors, etc.), which may require interactions among variables.


Correctly interpret your model parameters and inference


To compute predicted values, we need to remove the intercept from the selection model (𝛽𝛽0) and exponentiate the summed combinations of effects and variable values (𝑒𝑒(𝛽𝛽1×𝑋𝑋1+𝛽𝛽2×𝑋𝑋2…+𝛽𝛽𝑛𝑛∗𝑋𝑋𝑛𝑛)) where e can be implemented in R using the exp() function and the X1, X2,…Xn values are the new values of predictor variables (i.e., not the original data input into the model).
Inferring population density from habitat selection is most robust when there is auxiliary or additional validation of population density.


Decide whether model selection is necessary. It is reasonable to focus on fitting one model that captures all the variables that represent the complete hypotheses of interest. Do not assume model selection is a requirement.

The process for mapping and classifying seasonal migration corridors involves four primary steps:
1. Identify migration periods
To understand when an individual caribou is actually migrating (instead of just wandering around its seasonal range), we looked at how far it moves from a starting point over time. Using the Net Squared Displacement (NSD) method, which measures the straight-line distance an animal travels from a fixed starting point, we identified when an individual:

Leaves its winter or summer range,
Travels in a clear direction, and
Settles into the next seasonal range.

These “breakpoints” identify the start and end of each migration period. We identified them using the Movement Mapper app.
2. Map each caribou’s route
Instead of simply connecting caribou locations with a line, we used the Brownian Bridge Movement Model (BBMM) to create a more realistic “heat map” that highlights the areas an individual used most during its migration. Specifically, the map shows:

The likely corridor an individual followed, and
Where it spent extra time resting or feeding (stopovers).

3. Combine individual routes
To understand the movement the entire herd, we combined (stacked) individual maps through a three-step averaging process: 1. Average each individual’s migration paths over multiple years (e.g., 2020-26); 2. Identify the main area (footprint) where each caribou usually travels, typically representing the area containing 95-99% of its probable locations; 3. Combine all individuals’ footprints on top of one another to show how many different individuals passed through any given area (e.g., a 50m pixel).
4. Classify migration corridors
The final step is to classify the stacked maps (seasonal corridors) based on how heavily they were used:

Low use – at least one caribou passed through
Medium use – used by 10–20% of individuals
High use – used by more than 20% of individuals

We also identified key stopovers where caribou consistently paused to rest and feed. These are important areas to protect within the seasonal corridors.

Habitat covariates refer to the specific environmental and human factors used in statistical models (like HSFs) to predict habitat use and population health. For Northern Mountain Caribou, these variables are unique because of their reliance on rugged terrain and vertical migration.
Covariates can be grouped into four main categories:
1. Topographic & Environmental Covariates
Because Northern Mountain Caribou move vertically between seasons, elevation is the primary driver of their behavior.

Elevation: Used to track seasonal shifts (up to alpine areas in summer to avoid heat/insects, and down to sub-alpine forests in winter).

Slope and Aspect: Caribou often select steeper, wind-swept ridges in winter because the wind blows snow away, making it easier to reach lichens.

Snow Depth (SWE): A critical covariate for winter survival; excessive snow increases the metabolic cost of travel and limits access to food.

2. Forage & Vegetation Covariates
These identify the “food energy” available on the landscape.

Lichen Abundance: Specifically terrestrial lichens (Cladonia spp.) and arboreal lichens in old-growth forests.
Land Cover Type: Distinguishes between alpine tundra, sub-alpine fir, and spruce-lichen woodlands.
NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index): Used in summer to measure the “greenness” or quality of emerging forage, which is vital for lactating cows.

3. Disturbance Covariates (Anthropogenic & Natural)
These measure how much “space” caribou lose to human activity or environmental changes.

Distance to Roads/Infrastructure: Caribou show a strong “Zone of Influence” (ZOI) avoidance, often staying several kilometers away from active mines or high-use roads.

Linear Feature Density: The concentration of seismic lines or pipelines. Even if narrow, these act as “highways” for predators like wolves.

Fire Age: Caribou generally avoid burned areas for 40-60 years because fire destroys the slow-growing lichen they depend on.

4. Biological & Predation Covariates
These account for the “risk” on the landscape.

Predator Density/Risk: Often modeled as the probability of encountering wolves or bears.
Alternative Prey Density: Covariates for moose or deer are used to measure “apparent competition”?higher moose numbers often bring in more wolves, which then incidentally prey on caribou.

Reproductive State: Whether a cow has a calf significantly changes her selection; “cow-with-calf” is a common categorical covariate because these individuals prioritize safety (high elevation) over the best food.

Estimating the boundaries of seasonal and annual caribou ranges is an important step in effective wildlife conservation and management. Defining these spatial limits allows managers to identify core habitat areas, including calving grounds and winter foraging areas. This information is fundamental for land use planning, as it ensures that development and human activities are regulated to minimize disturbance and avoid habitat loss and fragmentation within these key areas. Ultimately, understanding and mapping caribou ranges provides the necessary baseline data to implement targeted conservation measures, monitor population health in relation to their environment, and support sustainable resource management for the long-term persistence of the herds.
We estimated annual and seasonal ranges using locations collected from many caribou over multiple years. To understand how herds use the landscape across the year, we grouped these locations into biologically meaningful seasons: annual, early winter, late winter, summer, and the fall rut. For each season, we used a statistical mapping approach called a kernel density estimator (KDE), implemented in R using the amt package. This method creates smooth contours around clusters of points, showing where caribou spend most of their time. The outer contour (the 95% isopleth) represents the broader seasonal range, while the inner contour (the 50% isopleth) highlights the core areas most heavily used.
This approach provides a consistent way to compare how different herds use space and how their ranges shift across seasons. Because it summarizes many individual movement paths into a single population‑level map, it helps identify key habitats and areas that may require conservation attention. The graphic below illustrates the concept, showing points, the estimated 95% range boundary, and the 50% core area for an example herd.
Individual-level range estimation
For each individual/year/season, use the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) method to estimate probability density functions of animal locations, resulting in utilization distributions.
Parameters: Select appropriate smoothing parameters (e.g., h-value) using methods like Likelihood Cross-Validation (LCV) or reference bandwidth.
Output: Generate 95% and 50% (or other relevant contours) utilization distributions (UDs) for annual and seasonal ranges for each individual for each year. The former (95%) represents the overall annual or seasonal range while the latter (50% isopleths) represents core or high use areas.
Population-level range estimation
There are two broad approaches that could be used to estimate population-level annual and seasonal ranges:

Method 1 - Union of individual ranges: Combine individual ranges (e.g., 95% KDEs) to visualize the total area used by the population annually and seasonally.
Method 2 - Population-level estimates: Pool all individual locations for a given period and estimate a single population-level range that represents the overall utilization distribution.

We used the second method to estimate population-level ranges and the resulting maps are available in the main section of the report (Section 9).
Interactive dashboard
In addition, to the maps in the report, we developed an interactive dashboard to assist in visualizing 1) individual- and population-level annual and seasonal range estimates and 2) variation in range estimates between individuals, years, and seasons.

Steps are computed per individual using steps(), which connects consecutive GPS fixes and calculates step length (sl_, in metres), turning angle (ta_, in radians), and time elapsed (dt_). Speed is derived as step length divided by duration.

Steps are computed per individual using steps(), which connects consecutive GPS fixes and calculates step length (sl_, in metres), turning angle (ta_, in radians), and time elapsed (dt_). Speed is derived as step length divided by duration.

  select(id, steps) |>

Introduction
Caribou play an important role for LFN, serving as a keystone species in local ecosystems and having cultural significance for Indigenous communities. Ecologically, caribou contribute to the health of boreal forests by influencing vegetation patterns and providing food for predators. Culturally, caribou provide food, materials for clothing and tools, and are a central part of local traditions and knowledge. Consequently, the conservation of their seasonal ranges, including winter foraging grounds and summer calving and grazing areas, is important for the health and long-term persistence of the population. However, these habitats are increasingly threatened by human activities and disturbances, particularly large-scale resource development like mining, which leads to habitat fragmentation and landscape alteration.
The establishment of Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs) and other protected lands are important tools for ensuring the long-term survival of caribou populations, as they allow for the management of these threats. These areas enable collaborative stewardship, respect traditional ecological knowledge, and support sustainable use, thus contributing to the persistence of caribou and their habitats. By prioritizing both ecological integrity and cultural continuity, IPCAs can thus strengthen conservation and sustainable land management now and in the future. As part of this project, we will evaluate the contribution of the proposed IPCAs to seasonal movements, habitat selection, and landscape connectivity.

title: Apps and Dashboards
text:
Apps
As part of the project, we are developing some interactive apps that can be used to support some of the analysis steps. The apps are intended to be general so that they can eventually be used for other study areas and species.
Movement Mapper:

Tool to assist in defining seasonal migration segments (periods)
Online: https://beaconsproject.shinyapps.io/movement_mapper
Github: https://github.com/beaconsproject/movement_mapper

Movement Explorer:

Tool to visualize movement data, define segments, estimate seasonal and annual ranges, and identify movement corridors. Note: for define segments, the Movement Mapper is preferred.
Online: https://beaconsproject.shinyapps.io/movement_explorer
Github: https://github.com/beaconsproject/movement_explorer

title: Apps and Dashboards
text:
Dashboards
To aid in visualizing and interpreting some of the components of the analysis, we are developing dashboards that can be used to view the results interactively. The four dashboards are linked together through menu buttons located at the top of each dashboard.

Movement data - Dashboard for visualizing caribou movement data and animations
Migration segments - Dashboard for visualizing the spring and fall migration segments that were defined using the Movement Mapper app.
Seasonal ranges - Dashboard for visualizing the output of the seasonal and annual ranges analysis
Seasonal corridors - Dashboard for visualing the output of the movement paths (corridors) analysis
